{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
[[File:Volume-Alhazen.svg|thumb|Layer cake representation.]]


In [[mathematics]], the '''layer cake representation''' of a non-[[negative number|negative]], [[real number|real]]-valued [[measurable function]] <math>f</math> defined on a [[measure space]] <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> is the formula

:<math>f(x) = \int_0^\infty 1_{L(f, t)} (x) \, \mathrm{d}t,</math>

for all <math>x \in \Omega</math>, where <math>1_E</math> denotes the [[indicator function]] of a subset <math>E\subseteq \Omega</math> and <math>L(f,t)</math> denotes the (strict) [[level set|super-level set]]:
:<math>
L(f, t) = \{ y \in \Omega \mid f(y) \geq t \}\;\;\;{\text{or}\;
L(f, t) = \{ y \in \Omega \mid f(y) > t \}}.
</math>
The layer cake representation follows easily from observing that
:<math> 1_{L(f, t)}(x) = 1_{[0, f(x)]}(t)\;\;\;
{\text{or}\;1_{L(f, t)}(x) = 1_{[0, f(x))}(t)}
</math>
where either integrand gives the same integral:
:<math>
f(x) = \int_0^{f(x)} \,\mathrm{d}t.
</math>
The [[layer cake]] representation takes its name from the representation of the value <math>f(x)</math> as the sum of contributions from the "layers" <math>L(f,t)</math>: "layers"/values <math>t</math> below <math>f(x)</math> contribute to the integral, while values <math>t</math> above <math>f(x)</math> do not.
It is a generalization of [[Cavalieri's principle]] and is also known under this name.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Willem |first1=Michel |title=Functional analysis : fundamentals and applications |date=2013 |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4614-7003-8}}</ref>{{rp|at=cor. 2.2.34}}

==Applications==
The layer cake representation can be used to rewrite the [[Lebesgue_integral#Via_improper_Riemann_integral|Lebesgue integral as an improper Riemann integral]]. For the measure space, <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math>, let <math>S\subseteq\Omega</math>, be a measureable subset (<math>S\in\mathcal{A})</math> and <math>f</math> a non-negative measureable function. By starting with the Lebesgue integral, then expanding <math>f(x)</math>, then exchanging integration order (see [[Fubini's theorem#Tonelli's theorem for non-negative measurable function|Fubini-Tonelli theorem]]) and simplifying in terms of the [[Lebesgue_integral#Indicator_functions|Lebesgue integral of an indicator function]], we get the [[Riemann integral]]:
:<math>
\begin{align}
\int_S f(x)\,\text{d}\mu(x) 
&= \int_S \int_0^\infty 1_{\{x\in\Omega\mid f(x)>t\}}(x)\,\text{d}t\,\text{d}\mu(x) \\
&= \int_0^\infty\!\! \int_S 1_{\{x\in\Omega\mid f(x)>t\}}(x)\,\text{d}\mu(x)\,\text{d}t\\
&= \int_0^\infty\!\! \int_\Omega 1_{\{x\in S\mid f(x)>t\}}(x)\,\text{d}\mu(x)\,\text{d}t\\
&= \int_0^{\infty} \mu(\{x\in S \mid f(x)>t\})\,\text{d}t.
\end{align}
</math>
This can be used in turn, to rewrite the integral for the [[Lp_space#Lp_spaces_and_Lebesgue_integrals|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>-space ''p''-norm]], for <math>1\leq p<+\infty</math>:
:<math>\int_\Omega |f(x)|^p \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x) = p\int_0^{\infty} s^{p-1}\mu(\{ x \in \Omega:|f(x)| > s \}) \mathrm{d}s,
</math>
which follows immediately from the change of variables <math>t=s^{p}</math> in the layer cake representation of <math>|f(x)|^p</math>. This representation can be used to prove [[Markov's inequality]] and [[Chebyshev's inequality]].
